new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (14 pp., text layer present; extracted text). PDF page 2 = printed p. 292, section 2 'Vocabularies', reads exactly: "Both vocabularies were written onto the cyclostyled questionnaire. Hale used a phonemic notation, which has been here transcribed according to a practical orthography, the main correspondences of which are given in Table 2." then Table 2 (Orthographic equivalents), then the standalone sentence "Stress is usually marked and is invariably on the first syllable." The quoted passage is verbatim at the stated locator. Surrounding section read: the sentence is a note on Hale's 1960 phonemic field notation that applies to both lists (78-item Parnkalla, Iron Knob, 6 March 1960…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Ken Hale's 1960 phonemic field transcription of the 91-item Karlamayi vocabulary (and the Parnkalla list recorded on the same trip), wherever stress was marked it fell on the first syllable of the word, without exception: primary stress is word-initial.
new_statements.exceptions: None: 'invariably on the first syllable'. 'Usually marked' refers to how often Hale wrote a stress mark in the notes, not to variation in placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Elicited citation forms only: 91 single words and short phrases recorded in a forty-minute session at Mukinbudin (WA) from the late Teddy Champion, 10 March 1960, written down by Hale (not tape-recorded). The sentence is an editorial note on the transcription conventions of both the Parnkalla and the Karlamayi lists, not a phonological analysis; no polysyllabic stress pattern, secondary stress or phrase-level prosody is described. Thieberger 1993:22-23 confirms no grammar or sketch grammar of Kalaamaya exists.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement concerns the 'Karlamayi' of the late Teddy Champion, recorded at Mukinbudin WA in 1960 and located by O'Grady at Moorine Rock, 15 mi W of Southern Cross; this is the Kalaamaya/Kalamaia (AIATSIS A4, ISO lkm) of Glottolog kala1401. Thieberger 1993 notes Oates 1975 reclassified it as a dialect of Wajarri, and Tindale gives Jawun/Kaburn as a north-western sub-name; Wikipedia treats Nyaki Nyaki (Njakinjaki) as a possible dialect, but Glottolog and Thieberger list Nyaki-Nyaki separately. The modern GALCAC spelling is Kaalamaya (language of the Kaprun/Gubrun people).
